messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark was thirty-six, a retail worker at a large department store in a midwestern suburb, married for eight years. He had been standing near the electronics counter when the man walked in with a rifle and began firing. The event lasted no more than two minutes, but for Mark it collapsed into a handful of snapshots: the flash of the first shot, a display of television screens shattering, a coworker’s body crumpling beside the registers. He lay flat on the floor, face pressed against the industrial carpet, and the texture of that rough weave—sticky with spilled soda and dust—burned into his senses. He could still feel it, days later, as if the fabric had transferred itself onto his palms.

In the weeks that followed, Mark found himself unable to shake the memory. The snapshots came back not as ordinary recollections but as moments that felt more real than the present: he would be stocking shelves and suddenly See the flash, Hear the pop, Taste the metallic tang of fear. What confused him most was the shame. He had done nothing wrong, yet when he remembered lying there while others died—or, worse, when he recalled the man who had kept firing, the moral violation of it, the complete disregard for human life—Mark felt a hot, private humiliation. He had not helped anyone. He had not even been brave. He had just stayed flat on the carpet, and the carpet was still with him.

His daily environment as a retail worker became a minefield. Physical proximity to other customers—crowds jostling in the aisles—made his chest tighten and brought the snapshots roaring back. Even worse were the moments when he saw people misbehaving: a shopper yelling at a cashier, a teenager stealing a candy bar, a small moral violation that felt to Mark like a re-enactment of the shooter’s disregard. And then there was the texture. When he touched anything rough and fibrous—the cardboard of a shipping box, a coworker’s wool sweater, the lining of his own jacket—the carpet came alive under his fingers, and he would freeze, lost in the memory.

He developed strategies to keep the memories at bay. He told himself the shooting had not really been that bad, that he was overreacting, that it must have been a different store, a different day. This magical thinking helped for a split second, but the denial only made the next trigger hit harder, because he had not allowed himself to process what happened. He tried hard not to think about the trauma at all—flipping channels when news of mass shootings appeared, refusing to talk about that afternoon with his wife. The suppression took effort, and the effort itself seemed to summon the very images he was trying to avoid. On the worst days, when the shame and the snapshots felt unbearable, he hurt himself physically: digging his fingernails into his forearm or punching his thigh, the sharp pain a momentary relief that stopped the memory from swallowing him whole. But afterward, the shame deepened, and the cycle tightened.

The more he suppressed, the more the memories felt intrusive and hyper-real. The more he used magical thinking, the more the triggers—crowds, moral lapses, rough textures—caught him off guard, because his mind refused to connect them to anything real. And each time a trigger landed, it reactivated the snapshot, fresh and vivid, as if the event were happening now. He began to avoid the area near the electronics counter at work, taking a longer route to the break room. He stopped going to the mall on weekends. When his wife asked what was wrong, he said nothing, because telling her would mean admitting it had happened, and his magical thinking fought against that admission.

Months afterward, Mark was still working the same job, but he was barely holding on. The self-harm had left bruises he hid under long sleeves. The shame had convinced him that he was weak, that he had failed a basic test of humanity. What finally brought him to a therapist’s office was not the pain or the fear—it was his wife’s quiet question, asked after he flinched away from her touch because she was wearing a sweater he could not bear to feel. “What happened to you that day?” she asked. And for the first time, Mark could not tell himself it had not happened. He sat in the waiting room, staring at the carpet—industrial, rough, beige—and waited to feel a panic that did not come. He hoped the therapist could help him make the snapshots ordinary again. He was terrified that they never would be.
